An elbow-length-sleeved boxy cotton T-shirt, a real plain T-shirt and not a real garment, covered edge to edge in an all-over sublimation print that covers the entire shirt, designed to make the shirt look like the outfit of a teacher. The design is enlarged to fill the entire shirt, edge to edge, with no blank margin around it. The outfit is printed across the whole front, over the shoulders and down both sleeves, showing a tweed jacket with chalk-dusted elbow patches. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. The outfit's fabric runs seamlessly over the shoulders and down the sleeves, every part of the shirt in the outfit's own colours and textures. The shirt keeps the outline of an ordinary T-shirt, round neckline, straight side seams, sleeves, and a straight open hem. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. The shirt's sleeves are tailored to end at the elbow, exactly where the outfit's sleeves end. Everything is flat ink on opaque cotton, lace, tulle, fur, feathers, sequins, armour and metal appear as printed patterns. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. The illusion is purely flat and two-dimensional, with no real fabric, buttons or pockets beyond the print. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces, the belt, straps and buckles of the outfit and the footwear's trim colours as stripes on the cuffs and hem, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for. Any printed skin, such as hands, wrists, neck, chest or forearms, is in a flat printed very deep brown skin tone.

The shirt's neckline is the outfit's collar opening, the shirt's sleeves carry the outfit's sleeves, and the shirt's hem is the outfit's lower edge, showing a white happi coat and a hachimaki headband. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's own cloth covers the whole shirt as one continuous print, so shoulders, sleeves and body are all in the outfit's colours. The shirt keeps the outline of an ordinary T-shirt, round neckline, straight side seams, sleeves, and a straight open hem. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The outfit's cloth runs unbroken from the collar band across both shoulders and down both sleeves to their hems, so every part of the shirt is outfit cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. A long-sleeved shirt is used so the outfit's long sleeves fit exactly, printed full length to the shirt's wrist hems. All textures, transparencies and sheens are printed patterns on solid cotton. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It also shows a printed collar around the real neckline. It is a trompe-l'oeil T-shirt, a plain cotton shirt pretending to be the outfit. It carries enough of the costume to be unmistakable, the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, the held item or gear of the outfit, shown as a patch or large motif on the chest or a sleeve and the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces, all in the outfit's own colours. Any printed skin, such as hands, wrists, neck, chest or forearms, is in a flat printed very deep brown skin tone.
